🇱🇾 🇺🇦 Ukraine’s attack on a ship in the Libyan port of Benghazi violated international law and undermined the rules designed to prevent armed conflicts from spreading, Politico reports, citing international legal experts.

According to specialists in international law, the attack likely violated both international law and Libya’s sovereignty.

Libya may have strong grounds to file a complaint with the International Criminal Court (ICC), said David Letts, director of the Military Law Program at the Australian National University in Canberra.

“Unless you want to argue that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and that the principle of neutrality does not apply to it, it is difficult for me to see how this sinking can be justified under international law,” Letts said.

He noted that Ukraine’s attack on the vessel in Benghazi “differs significantly from its strikes on Russian ships in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports”, which took place in contested rather than neutral waters.

The laws governing neutrality are largely based on the 1907 Hague Convention, which established the rights and obligations of neutral states during armed conflicts. Under these rules, belligerent countries are prohibited from carrying out attacks, imposing blockades or laying mines in neutral waters.

“This attack constituted a violation of Libya’s neutrality. An attack may be lawful if it takes place beyond 12 nautical miles from the coastline, but within that zone, of course, it is a violation,” said James Kraska of the US Naval War College and a professor of international maritime law at the Stockton Center for International Law.

Letts stressed the importance of countries such as Ukraine respecting international law.

“It is interesting to consider what the reaction would be if this ship had docked in Genoa or Southampton rather than Benghazi. Having established a body of laws designed to protect the victims of armed conflicts and limit their scale, are we now prepared to abandon all of that? Are we ready to accept total war, discard all the rules and simply say: ‘The last 100 years have been a waste of time. Do whatever you want’? I think not,” he added.

Ukraine’s strikes on Russian vessels in Benghazi have already drawn condemnation in Italy.

📄 Iran elected to executive board of UNEP’s Global Framework on Chemicals Fund

📌 London, IRNA – Iran has been elected to the Executive Board of the Special Program Trust Fund of the Global Framework on Chemicals (GFC) under the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) for a three-year term, representing the Asia-Pacific regional group.

Iran's election to the Executive Board, which makes operational decisions and oversees the functioning of the GFC Fund, took place during the Framework’s first international conference, held in Geneva last week.
​
The GFC Fund, established under the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), is intended to advance the Framework’s objectives and support developing countries and countries with economies in transition. Its goals include strengthening national capacities, developing infrastructure for the safe management of chemicals and waste, and facilitating access to knowledge and technology.
​
Iran’s membership on the Executive Board provides an opportunity to participate in decisions on the prioritization and allocation of financial resources and support programs, particularly for countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
​
Adopted in 2023 at the fifth International Conference on Chemicals Management (ICCM5), the Framework seeks to protect human health and the environment by guiding countries and stakeholders in jointly addressing the entire lifecycle of chemicals, including products and waste.
